Acceleration: When Velocity Changes

We treated velocity as staying the same. How close was that to the real motion?

Velocity tells how fast something moves and in which direction. Watch for two ways it can change: a car can speed up or it can turn.

The asteroid thread

What we know so far

Today

text:

Slowing down is accelerating, too.

When an object slows, acceleration points against its motion. If motion is positive, this acceleration is negative.

title: Earth’s pull at the starting separation
text:
Back to **2026**-XJ

≈ **13 min**

**How much** does Earth pull on it right now?

Distancer = **1.2 × 10⁸ km** = **1.2 × 10¹¹ m**

Earth's pulla = GM ÷ r²

Resulta ≈ **2.8 × 10⁻⁸ m/s²**

This estimate uses only Earth’s pull at this distance. It leaves out the Sun. It does not prove a long-term prediction is right.

Read r as the distance between the centers of Earth and the asteroid. Use meters in the formula. The result tells how much Earth alone changes the asteroid’s velocity each second at that distance.

teachingStep: Look at the distance in the bottom of the gravity formula. A smaller distance makes the pull stronger. Recheck the distance before using the same acceleration later.
title: Gravity changes along the path
text:
Looking ahead

≈ **13 min**

As **2026**-XJ gets closer, gravity gets stronger.

We used steady velocity to make the math simpler. Gravity changes along the path. Unit **2** adds this effect.

Look at the distance in the bottom of the gravity formula. A smaller distance makes the pull stronger. Recheck the distance before using the same acceleration later.

teachingStep: Follow the estimate in the panel: multiply the change each second by the number of seconds. This works if the pull stays steady. Over a long trip, both distance and pull can change.
title: A small change is still a change
text:
**2026**-XJ · **What Changes** · Graphic novel, page **28**

A small change is still a change

This class estimate uses Earth’s pull only. Acceleration is 2.8 times ten to the minus eight meters per second squared. If it stays the same for 1.6 times ten to the seven seconds, velocity changes by about 0.448 meters each second. Mr. Antocci says the Sun’s effect is bigger here. Gravity also changes along the path.

This estimate is for a made-up story. It works only if the stated choices hold. It does not predict the whole orbit.

What are we treating as true? What must we check before using this estimate for a long time?

Part **3** · Check what the estimate tells us · Write your own answer in Work.

Follow the estimate in the panel: multiply the change each second by the number of seconds. This works if the pull stays steady. Over a long trip, both distance and pull can change.
